title: Preregistered Paired Evaluation of a Deterministic Verifier Pipeline for LLM‑Generated Network Configuration Changes
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment that tested whether deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → optional repair) changes the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe network‑change proposals produced by a hosted LLM on intent→configuration NetOps tasks. Design: N=200 synthetic, preregistered tasks in a paired design comparing (a) baseline LLM‑only and (b) guarded pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5) using shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (one initial LLM candidate generated per task and shared between arms). Key observed quantities (adversarial cluster): baseline unsafe proposals = 0/200; guarded unsafe proposals = 0/200 (paired contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0). Computed estimand (analysis artifacts used 1 = SAFE, i.e., reported quantities are differences in safe‑rates): guarded minus baseline safe‑rate = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (resamples=10000, seed=1729). Crucial clarification and methodological diagnosis: the preregistered confirmatory hypothesis (a verifier‑caused reduction in unsafe proposals) could not be meaningfully tested under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with a ceilinged task bank (baseline unsafe rate observed = 0%), and the run used model_calls_used = 200 (one generation per pair) rather than the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400. We correct an archival labeling inconsistency: the preregistration defined the per‑arm binary indicator as 1 = unsafe, but the archived analysis and scoring artifacts use 1 = SAFE; the manuscript therefore reports the computed paired difference in SAFE rates (mapping to the preregistered unsafe‑rate difference is described in Methods). We archive execution and analysis artifacts and recommend an independent per‑arm generation design, stronger adversarial templates, and multi‑model coverage for future confirmatory tests.

sections.introduction: Automating intent→configuration translation with large language models (LLMs) can reduce operator workload but raises operational safety concerns: incorrect network changes may break reachability, violate policy, or cause outages. Prior work advocates tool‑augmentation (deterministic validators, sandboxed replay, approval gates) and generate–verify–refine pipelines to improve trust in agentic NetOps. We asked one specific, preregistered question: How does deterministic tool‑augmentation (generate → deterministic verifier/sandbox → automatic refinement) change the rate of verifier‑detected unsafe configuration proposals produced by a hosted LLM under benign and adversarial NetOps prompts? Contributions: (1) a machine‑readable preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (N=200 synthetic tasks) comparing baseline LLM‑only to a guarded pipeline; (2) archived execution and deterministic analysis showing both arms returned zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals under the executed conditions and a concise correction of an archival labeling mismatch (analysis used 1 = SAFE); (3) a focused methodological diagnosis that the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics plus a ceilinged task bank made the confirmatory paired test non‑informative, with concrete recommendations for repeat preregistered designs.
sections.related_work: Surveys and prototypes document rapid adoption of LLMs in NetOps (intent translation, config synthesis, AIOps co‑pilots) and repeatedly recommend verifier/tool grounding for high‑stakes changes. Representative works describe architectures and benchmarks advocating tool‑grounded evaluation and generate–verify–refine loops; others study guardrails and red‑teaming for agentic systems. These studies show tool‑augmentation can improve measured correctness in controlled settings, but gains depend on task difficulty, verifier fidelity, adversarial coverage, and evaluation workflow. Our study aimed to provide preregistered, workflow‑centred evidence focused on verifier impact under a paired design and deterministic sandbox scoring.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The machine‑readable preregistration (frozen before execution) specified a paired binary design with primary estimand originally named paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (preregister text described an unsafe‑rate difference). Sampling: a deterministic generator produced 200 synthetic intent→configuration tasks (single‑AS, multi‑device topologies; intent types: IPv4 reachability, ACL/policy preservation, ordered safety workflows). Model and orchestration: declared model = gpt‑5‑mini served via the project's adapter; guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as a sandboxed intent/constraint validator. Generation semantics and model‑call accounting: preregistration allowed shared_initial_candidate semantics; the executed run set independent_condition_generation=false so each paired task used a single shared initial LLM candidate that both arms received (the guarded arm handed that candidate to the deterministic validator). Consequence: model_calls_used = 200 (one generation per task, shared across arms) rather than the preregistered maximum_model_calls = 400 (independent per‑arm generation). Execution and analysis artifacts: completed_episode_count = 400, complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200; execution artifacts include execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, and execution/execution_manifest.json and analysis artifacts include analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv (all archived in the supplied bundle). Binary‑labeling correction and estimand mapping: the preregistration text used ambiguous naming; the archived analysis and scoring encoded per‑arm binary outcomes with code 1 = SAFE (no verifier‑detected violation) and 0 = UNSAFE. Therefore the archived computed estimand equals the paired difference in SAFE rates (guarded_safe_rate − baseline_safe_rate). Mapping to the preregistered (unsafe‑rate) estimand: paired_diff_unsafe = − (paired_diff_safe). All numeric results reported below follow the archived code (1 = SAFE) and we explicitly present this mapping.
sections.results: Execution accounting: planned episodes = 400 (200 pairs) and all were completed; model_calls_used = 200; failed episodes = 0. Scoring rule: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 validated final configurations in sandbox and produced binary indicators (1 = SAFE, 0 = UNSAFE). Observed confirmatory counts (adversarial cluster reported here): baseline SAFE successes = 200/200; guarded SAFE successes = 200/200. Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 200 (both safe), n10 = 0 (guarded safe, baseline unsafe), n01 = 0 (guarded unsafe, baseline safe), n00 = 0 (both unsafe). Computed quantity (guarded_safe_rate − baseline_safe_rate) = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (percentile bootstrap, resamples = 10000, seed = 1729). No verifier refusals or discordant pairs occurred, so preregistered exploratory refusal/ROC diagnostics produced no informative estimates. Representative artifacts: analysis/condition_summary.csv and analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv summarize these counts; execution/execution_manifest.json records model_calls_used and episode accounting.
sections.discussion: Statistical and causal interpretation: the observed contingency (zero discordant pairs) implies the paired test was non‑informative for the preregistered causal hypothesis under the executed generation semantics. Mechanism: shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical initial candidates for baseline and guarded arms; when those shared candidates were already valid for the declared model, the deterministic validator had no opportunity to reject or repair, producing n10 = n01 = 0. This outcome also created a ceiling effect: the observed baseline unsafe rate = 0% (contrasting preregistered power assumptions that assumed a ~10–15% baseline unsafe rate), invalidating the preregistered power calculation. Practical implications: (1) to measure a verifier’s causal effect on unsafe proposals, independent per‑arm generation is required so the validator can act on model outputs that would otherwise be different between arms; (2) task banks must be constructed (or adversarial templates strengthened) to produce nonzero baseline unsafe rates for the target model; (3) multi‑model testing and verifier stress tests (obfuscation, adversarial transforms) are needed to evaluate false‑negative/false‑positive trade‑offs. Recommendations for a repeat preregistered confirmatory study (archived artifacts enable reproducible follow‑ups): preregister independent per‑arm generation, increase adversarial strength and task difficulty to avoid ceiling effects, enlarge model diversity beyond a single declared model, and include explicit verifier ROC exploratory arms.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment comparing LLM‑only versus a deterministic verifier‑augmented pipeline on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM candidate per task shared across arms) and for the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini), both arms produced zero verifier‑detected unsafe proposals (paired difference in SAFE rates = 0.0; p = 1.0). Crucially, the preregistered causal hypothesis about verifier‑driven reductions in unsafe proposals could not be meaningfully tested because shared per‑pair generation removed the opportunity for the verifier to change outcomes when the shared candidate was already valid; furthermore the observed baseline unsafe rate (0%) contradicted the preregistered power assumptions. The principal scientific outcome is thus methodological: preregistration choices (generation semantics and task difficulty) determine whether a verifier effect can be observed; future confirmatory tests should use independent per‑arm generation, stronger adversarial tasks, and model diversity. All execution and analysis artifacts are archived for reproducible follow‑ups (see execution and analysis artifact paths).

limitations: Synthetic‑task domain and coverage: tasks were deterministic synthetic topologies limited to single‑AS multi‑device setups (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5); results may not generalize to production, multi‑AS, or vendor‑specific features.

Shared‑generation semantics: the preregistered design used shared_initial_candidate per paired task (independent_condition_generation = false). This produced identical initial candidates for baseline and guarded arms, creating a ceiling effect when those candidates were valid and preventing observation of verifier‑driven differences.

Adversarial prompt strength: although an adversarial cluster was preregistered, the adversarial templates used in this run did not elicit unsafe outputs from gpt‑5‑mini on the sampled tasks; stronger and more diverse adversarial cases are needed.
Single‑model scope: only the declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) was evaluated; no claims of multi‑model generality are supported.

Verifier validation scope: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 operated deterministically on archived synthetic sandboxed states; external independent validation of validator completeness against all real‑world NetOps failure modes is not provided.

Operational external validity: no production deployment, operator‑in‑the‑loop workload measurement, nor multi‑vendor interoperability field trials were performed; operator‑cost trade‑offs (false refusals, extra verification workload) remain unquantified at scale.
